lessons.title: Wellness is more than not being ill
cards: Feeling well is broader than having no illness.
The book's framing: you can be physically fit and still not feel well if other parts of life are struggling.
It invites you to look at your life as a whole, not one area at a time.
lessons.tryThis: Take five quiet minutes tonight. On paper, list the eight OneUP dimensions. Next to each, write one word for how that area feels today, such as 'steady', 'tired' or 'ignored'. Circle the area that feels least well. Then choose one small, easy action for it tomorrow, something that takes ten minutes or less, and write down when you will do it.

body.intro: Most of us learn to think about health in a simple way: if nothing hurts and the doctor has no complaints, we must be fine. Yet many people know the odd feeling of being 'not ill' and still not feeling well. This lesson looks at the broader idea of wellness that sits behind The Wellness 8 as its publisher describes it, and behind OneUP's own eight dimensions. Note: these lessons are based only on the publisher's description of The Wellness 8 [VERIFY]. They explain a general wellness model in our own words and do not claim to reproduce what the book says.
sections: Health and wellness are not the same word

Health is often described by what is missing: no fever, no injury, no worrying test result. Wellness, in the way many wellness models use the word, is described by what is present: energy for the day, relationships that feel supportive, work that feels meaningful, a sense of calm about money and surroundings. The two overlap a great deal, but they are not identical. Someone can have a clean bill of health and still feel flat, lonely or stuck. Someone else can be living with a long-term condition and still feel that many parts of life are going well.

Thinking in terms of wellness does not replace medical care. It simply widens the lens so that you notice more of your life at once.
Why the whole picture matters

Areas of life tend to lean on each other. Poor sleep can make patience thin, which can strain a friendship, which can make it harder to focus at work. Money worries can quietly affect sleep. A cluttered room can make it harder to rest. Because of these links, improving one area sometimes eases another, and neglecting one area can drag others down.

A whole-life view helps you avoid a common trap: pouring all your effort into one area, such as fitness or career, while other areas slowly wear thin without you noticing.
Wellness as a direction, not a finish line

A helpful way to hold this idea is to treat wellness as something you move towards rather than something you either have or lack. Every area has good weeks and hard weeks. The aim is not to score perfectly everywhere, which nobody does, but to notice where you are and choose a small next step.

This framing is gentler. It replaces 'Am I healthy or not?' with 'Which part of my life could use a little care right now?' That question is easier to act on, and it leaves room for the fact that life changes.
What this does not mean

A wider view of wellness is not a diagnosis tool, and it is not a reason to ignore symptoms. If something in your body or mood worries you, a qualified professional is the right person to talk to. A wellness model is a way to reflect and plan everyday habits, nothing more and nothing less.

example.title: Illustrative example: Meera's 'fine' month
example.text: Meera, a software tester in Pune, had a routine check-up and every result came back normal. She was relieved, yet she still felt drained most evenings. When she looked at her life area by area, a pattern appeared. Her body was fine, but she had not called her close friends in weeks, her desk was buried under papers, and she felt uneasy because she had no idea where her salary went each month. None of these was a medical problem. Together, they explained why 'healthy' did not feel like 'well'. She chose one small step, a Sunday call with a friend, and noticed the week felt lighter. This is an illustrative story, not a real case.

takeaways: Health often means the absence of illness; wellness looks at what is present in your life.
Areas of life influence each other, so a whole-life view catches problems early.
Treat wellness as a direction you move in, not a test you pass or fail.
A wellness model supports reflection; it does not replace professional care.
reflect: When did you last feel 'healthy' but not 'well'? What was missing?
Which area of your life tends to get ignored when you are busy?

lessons.title: A wheel with eight spokes
cards: The book names eight areas: emotional, environmental, financial, intellectual, occupational, physical, social and spiritual.
It compares them to spokes on a wheel: if one is weak, the whole ride feels bumpy.
Balance doesn't mean perfect scores; it means no spoke is forgotten.
lessons.tryThis: Draw a simple circle with eight spokes and label each with a OneUP dimension. Rate each area from one to five and mark the score on its spoke, then join the dots. Look at the shape. Pick the loosest spoke and write one small step you could take for it this week. Keep the drawing and redo it in a month to see what changed.

body.intro: Picture a bicycle wheel. When every spoke is strong, the ride is smooth. When a few spokes are loose, the wheel wobbles even if the rest are fine. Many wellness models use a wheel like this to show how different parts of life hold each other up. The publisher describes The Wellness 8 as being organised around eight dimensions of wellness [VERIFY exact list], and OneUP is organised around eight dimensions as well. Note: these lessons are based only on the publisher's description of The Wellness 8 [VERIFY]. They explain a general wellness model in our own words and do not claim to reproduce what the book says.
sections: The eight spokes in OneUP

OneUP uses eight dimensions: physical, emotional, social, spiritual, intellectual, occupational, environmental and financial. Physical covers the body: movement, rest and food. Emotional covers how you notice and handle feelings. Social is about connection and belonging. Spiritual is about meaning, values and what feels bigger than daily tasks, whether or not that involves religion. Intellectual is about curiosity and learning. Occupational is about work, study or any role that fills your days. Environmental is about the spaces you live and work in. Financial is about your relationship with money and the sense of security around it.

Different books and organisations name and group these areas slightly differently. The labels matter less than the habit of looking at all of them.
Why a wheel and not a ladder

A ladder suggests you climb one rung at a time and leave the lower ones behind. A wheel suggests that every part keeps mattering at once. You never 'finish' the physical spoke and move on to the social one. Instead, attention shifts around the wheel as life changes. During exams, the intellectual spoke may take most of your energy. After a move to a new city, the social and environmental spokes may need more care.
Balance does not mean equal

It is tempting to think a balanced wheel means spending the same time on every area. In practice that is neither possible nor necessary. Balance here means that no spoke is so neglected that it makes the whole ride wobble. A busy parent might give very little time to hobbies for a while, and that can be perfectly fine, as long as it is a conscious choice and not a slow drift.

A quick self-check, rating each area from one to five, can show which spoke is loosest. That loosest spoke is often the best place for a small next step.
Using the wheel without judging yourself

Low scores are information, not a verdict on your worth. Everyone has areas that are harder for them, and those can change from month to month. The point of the wheel is to guide attention kindly, not to create another list of things to feel guilty about.

example.title: Illustrative example: Arjun's loose spoke
example.text: Arjun, a final-year engineering student in Chennai, rated himself on all eight dimensions one evening. Intellectual and occupational were high because of placements. Physical was middling. Social was a one: he had stopped joining his friends for evening tea since exams began. He realised the loneliness was making him more anxious about results. He did not quit studying; he simply joined the tea break twice a week. The wheel did not tell him what to do. It showed him where to look. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: A wellness wheel shows that areas of life support each other.
OneUP uses eight dimensions; other models group them slightly differently.
Balance means no area is badly neglected, not that every area gets equal time.
Low scores point to where a small step may help most.
reflect: If you rated each of the eight areas from one to five today, which would be lowest?
Is that low area a conscious trade-off right now, or a slow drift?

lessons.title: Keep learning, even when busy
cards: The book encourages a habit of continuous learning.
Learning doesn't need long blocks of time; small, regular amounts add up.
Curiosity can be practised like any other habit.
lessons.tryThis: Choose one topic you are genuinely curious about. Find one short source on it, such as a ten-minute video, a podcast episode or a few pages of a book. Schedule it into a gap you already have, like a commute or tea break, on three days this week. Afterwards, tell one person one thing you learned.

body.intro: Learning is easy to associate with school and college, something that ends when a degree certificate arrives. Yet curiosity does not have an expiry date. The publisher's description of The Wellness 8 includes ongoing learning as part of a well life [VERIFY]. This lesson explores, in general terms, why intellectual wellness matters even when life is busy. Note: these lessons are based only on the publisher's description of The Wellness 8 [VERIFY]. They explain a general wellness model in our own words and do not claim to reproduce what the book says.
sections: What intellectual wellness means

Intellectual wellness is about keeping your mind engaged. That can mean reading, picking up a skill, asking questions, solving puzzles, having a good debate, or exploring a subject purely for the joy of it. It is not about being clever or having degrees. A grandmother learning to video-call her grandchildren is exercising this dimension just as much as a researcher writing a paper.
Why learning feels good

Many people notice that learning something new brings a quiet sense of satisfaction. It can make the days feel less repetitive, give you fresh things to talk about, and build confidence that you can handle unfamiliar situations. Learning also tends to spill into other dimensions. A new cooking skill touches the physical dimension. A course related to your job touches the occupational one. Learning a little about budgeting touches the financial one.
The busy-life problem

The usual reason people stop learning is not lack of interest but lack of time and energy. After work, commuting and household duties, a long course can feel impossible. The answer is usually to make learning smaller rather than to give it up. Ten minutes of reading before bed, a podcast during a commute, or one new recipe a week all count. Small, regular learning often adds up to more than occasional bursts of enthusiasm that fade.
Learning with others

Learning does not have to be solitary. Discussing a book with a friend, joining a local class, or teaching a younger relative something you know can make learning more enjoyable and help it stick. Explaining an idea to someone else is also a good way to find out how well you really understand it.
Making it a habit

Learning sticks best when it has a regular place in your week. You might link it to something you already do, such as reading a few pages with your morning tea, or keeping a small notebook of interesting things you came across each day. Another helpful idea is to follow your own curiosity rather than what you think you should learn. Interest makes it much easier to keep going, and keeping going matters more than the size of each session. Over months, these small sessions quietly build knowledge and confidence.

example.title: Illustrative example: Lakshmi's commute library
example.text: Lakshmi spends about forty minutes each way on a Mumbai local train. For months she scrolled social media on the journey and arrived home feeling scattered. She decided to try one change: on the morning ride she would listen to an episode of an educational podcast about history, a subject she had loved in school. She did not set any target. After a few weeks, she found she was looking forward to the commute and chatting with her teenage son about what she had heard. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Intellectual wellness is about curiosity and engagement, not intelligence or qualifications.
Learning can lift mood and spill into other dimensions of life.
When time is short, make learning smaller instead of stopping it.
Learning with or teaching others makes it more enjoyable and memorable.
reflect: What is something you were curious about as a child that you have not explored in years?
Where in your week is there a small pocket of time that could hold ten minutes of learning?

lessons.title: The value of kindness
cards: The book highlights kindness and contributing to others as part of being well.
Small acts count: a message, a thank-you, a moment of attention.
Kindness tends to strengthen the relationships around you.
lessons.tryThis: Today, do one small, specific act of kindness for someone you usually overlook, such as learning their name or thanking them properly. Tonight, also notice one moment when you spoke harshly to yourself, and quietly rewrite that sentence the way you would say it to a good friend. Note both in a line or two.

body.intro: Kindness is often described as something we do for others. It can also be part of how we look after our own wellbeing. The publisher's description of The Wellness 8 touches on kindness and contribution [VERIFY]. This lesson explores, in general terms, how giving and receiving kindness connects to social and emotional wellness. Note: these lessons are based only on the publisher's description of The Wellness 8 [VERIFY]. They explain a general wellness model in our own words and do not claim to reproduce what the book says.
sections: Kindness as connection

Every act of kindness, however small, creates a moment of connection. Holding a door, thanking the security guard by name, sending a message to a friend who has had a tough week: these small acts remind both people that they are not alone. Social wellness grows from many such moments, not only from big gatherings or close friendships.
Why giving can feel good

Many people notice that helping someone else lifts their own mood. Doing something for another person can shift attention away from our own worries for a while and give a sense of purpose. That feeling is a natural part of being a social creature. It is worth noticing, though, that kindness offered only to feel good about ourselves can become a performance. The most nourishing kindness tends to come from genuine care.
Kindness that includes yourself

Kindness is not only outward. The way you speak to yourself after a mistake matters too. Many people are far gentler with friends than with themselves. Practising the same patience inward, such as saying 'That was hard, and I did my best' instead of harsh self-criticism, is part of emotional wellness. Self-kindness is not the same as making excuses; it simply means not adding extra pain to a difficult moment.
Kindness with boundaries

Being kind does not mean saying yes to everything. Constantly giving without rest can lead to resentment and exhaustion. Healthy kindness includes limits: helping when you can, saying no honestly when you cannot, and accepting help from others in return. Receiving kindness gracefully is also a gift to the person offering it.
Starting small

You do not need grand gestures to practise kindness. A sincere thank-you, remembering someone's name, listening without checking your phone, or sharing food with a neighbour are all forms of it. Some people find it helpful to notice one kind act they did and one they received at the end of each day. This is not about keeping score. It simply trains attention towards the warmth that is already present in ordinary life, which can be easy to overlook on a busy or difficult day.

example.title: Illustrative example: the building watchman
example.text: Rohit had lived in his Bengaluru apartment block for two years without learning the night watchman's name. One evening, returning late and tired, he stopped to ask. The watchman, Suresh, told him he had a daughter starting college. Over the next months, their brief chats became something Rohit looked forward to. Nothing dramatic changed, but Rohit noticed he felt more at home in the building, and Suresh seemed to feel more seen. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Small acts of kindness create moments of connection that support social wellness.
Helping others can give a sense of purpose, especially when it comes from genuine care.
Kindness includes how you speak to yourself.
Healthy kindness has boundaries and includes receiving help too.
reflect: Who is someone you see often but have never really spoken to?
How do you usually talk to yourself after a mistake? Would you say the same to a friend?

lessons.title: Small changes compound
cards: Tiny improvements feel insignificant on any single day.
Repeated over months, they add up to a large difference, in either direction.
Look at the direction you're heading, not just today's result.
lessons.tryThis: Pick one habit you have been meaning to build. Shrink it to a version so small it feels almost silly, such as one push-up, one page or one minute of tidying. Do that tiny version every day for two weeks, and put a mark on a calendar each time. Focus on the streak, not the size.

body.intro: When we want to change our lives, we often look for one big move: a strict new diet, a dramatic new routine, a resolution that will fix everything at once. Atomic Habits begins from the opposite direction. Its central argument is that small, almost unnoticeable improvements, repeated consistently, can add up to large changes over time. This lesson summarises ideas from Atomic Habits by James Clear in our own words.
sections: Why small feels pointless at first

A tiny improvement rarely produces a visible result on the day you make it. Reading five pages does not make you wise by evening. One healthy meal does not change your body by morning. Because the reward is not immediate, small actions are easy to dismiss as not worth the effort. The book points out that this is exactly why many people give up on good habits too early: they expect quick results from changes that only show their value over time.
The idea of compounding

The book borrows the idea of compounding, familiar from savings, to describe habits. When a small gain builds on yesterday's small gain, the effect grows over time instead of simply adding up. The same works in reverse. Small negative choices, such as skipping sleep or putting off one task, can also compound quietly. The message is not that every moment is critical, but that the direction you are heading in matters a great deal more than any single day.
The plateau before the breakthrough

The book describes a frustrating stage where you are putting in effort but seeing little change. It compares progress to ice warming slowly in a cold room: nothing seems to happen until, at a certain point, it starts to melt. Earlier effort was not wasted; it was building up. Understanding this stage can help you keep going when results seem invisible, instead of concluding that the habit 'does not work'.
Trajectory over results

Because small habits take time to show results, the book suggests paying attention to your trajectory rather than your current position. Someone with modest savings who saves a little each month may be on a better path than someone with more money who spends it all. Someone who is unfit but walking every day may be heading somewhere better than someone fitter who has stopped moving. Asking 'Which way am I heading?' is often more useful than 'Where am I now?'
What this means for you

The practical lesson is to make your next improvement smaller than you think it needs to be, and then repeat it. Small changes are easier to start, easier to keep, and less likely to collapse on a busy day. Over weeks and months, they can reshape routines in a way that dramatic bursts of effort often cannot.

example.title: Illustrative example: Priya's five pages
example.text: Priya, a bank employee in Ahmedabad, wanted to read more but kept buying books she never finished. She decided to read just five pages each night after dinner, no more required. Some nights she read more, some nights only the five. For the first few weeks it felt like almost nothing. By the end of a few months she realised she had finished several books, more than in the previous year. The change came from consistency, not effort. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Small improvements can add up to large changes when repeated over time.
Results from good habits are often delayed, which is why people quit too early.
Progress can feel invisible before it becomes visible; keep going through the plateau.
Watch your direction of travel more than your current position.
reflect: Which habit did you give up on because it did not show results quickly enough?
What direction is one area of your life heading in, if nothing changes?

lessons.title: Systems over goals
cards: Goals describe the result you want; systems are the everyday processes that get you there.
People with the same goal can get very different results because their systems differ.
Improving the process often matters more than restating the target.
lessons.tryThis: Write down one goal you care about. Underneath, write the system that would move you towards it in one sentence: 'I will [action] at [time] in [place].' Make the action small enough for a busy day. Follow the system for one week, ticking each day you show up, and judge yourself only by the ticks.

body.intro: Most advice about change begins with goals: lose weight, save money, get a promotion. Atomic Habits argues that goals are useful for setting a direction, but that the real work happens in systems, the daily processes that lead to results. This lesson explores the difference and why it matters. This lesson summarises ideas from Atomic Habits by James Clear in our own words.
sections: Goals versus systems

A goal is the result you want. A system is the set of habits and routines that produce results. If your goal is a clean room, your system might be putting things away each evening. If your goal is to pass an exam, your system might be a daily study block. The book's point is that people with the same goal can get very different results because their systems differ. The goal alone does not create the change; the system does.
Why goals alone can fall short

The book raises a few problems with relying on goals alone. Winners and losers often share the same goals, so the goal cannot be what separates them. Reaching a goal is only a moment; if the system that got you there stops, the result can fade. Goals can also make happiness feel postponed: 'I will be content once I reach it'. And once a goal is achieved, motivation can disappear, leaving people to slip back to old patterns.
Falling in love with the process

A systems approach shifts attention from the finish line to the daily practice. Instead of measuring yourself only by whether you reached a target, you ask whether you showed up for the routine today. This tends to be more satisfying, because you can succeed every day you follow the process, rather than only on the day you reach a goal. It also encourages long-term thinking: the system can keep running after any single goal is met.
Designing a simple system

A simple system usually answers three questions: what will I do, when will I do it, and where? For example: 'I will walk for twenty minutes after lunch, around the office building.' The system should be small enough to survive busy days. It can be adjusted over time as you learn what works. The goal stays in the background as a compass, while the system does the daily work.
Systems in money and work

This idea applies well beyond fitness. At work, a system might be clearing your inbox at set times instead of reacting all day. With money, it might be noting expenses every Sunday, or moving a fixed amount to savings on payday so you do not have to decide each month. These examples are illustrative only, and money decisions should be based on your own situation. This is not financial advice.

example.title: Illustrative example: the exam system
example.text: Rahul, a commerce student in Jaipur, set a goal of scoring well in his accountancy exam. In past years he had studied in panicked bursts just before tests. This time he set a system: one hour of practice problems every evening at his desk, starting right after dinner. Some evenings went badly, but the routine held. By exam week he felt calmer, not because the goal had changed but because the system had been doing the work quietly for months. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Goals set direction; systems are the daily processes that create results.
Goals alone can postpone happiness and fade once reached.
Focusing on the process lets you succeed every day you show up.
A good system says what, when and where, and is small enough for busy days.
reflect: Think of a goal you have. What daily system would move you towards it?
Have you ever reached a goal and then slipped back? What system was missing?

lessons.title: Habits shape who you become
cards: Lasting change is easier when it's tied to the kind of person you want to be.
Each time you act in line with that identity, you add evidence that it's true.
Ask 'Who do I want to become?' as well as 'What do I want to achieve?'
lessons.tryThis: Complete this sentence: 'I am the kind of person who…' with an identity you want, such as 'moves every day' or 'keeps promises to myself'. Then list three small actions that would be votes for that identity. Do one today. Each evening this week, count how many votes you cast.

body.intro: Why do some habits stick while others fade? Atomic Habits suggests that the deepest layer of change is not what you do or what you achieve, but who you believe you are. This lesson explores the idea of identity-based habits: building habits around the kind of person you want to become. This lesson summarises ideas from Atomic Habits by James Clear in our own words.
sections: Three layers of change

The book describes change happening at three levels. The outer layer is outcomes, such as losing weight or writing a book. The middle layer is processes, the habits and routines you follow. The inner layer is identity, your beliefs about yourself. Many people start with outcomes: 'I want to run a marathon.' The book suggests starting from identity instead: 'I am a person who moves my body every day.'
Why identity makes habits stick

When a habit is tied to identity, it becomes less about willpower and more about being consistent with yourself. Compare two people offered a cigarette. One says, 'No thanks, I'm trying to quit.' The other says, 'No thanks, I don't smoke.' The first still sees themselves as a smoker resisting temptation. The second has shifted identity. The book uses examples like this to show how the story we tell about ourselves shapes our choices.
Every action is a vote

A helpful idea from the book is that each action is like a vote for the kind of person you want to be. Reading one page is a vote for being a reader. Tidying your desk is a vote for being an organised person. You do not need a unanimous vote; you just need more votes for the identity you want than against it. This takes the pressure off any single day: a missed workout is one vote, not a verdict.
Choosing your identity

The book suggests a two-step process: decide the type of person you want to be, then prove it to yourself with small wins. Asking 'What would a healthy person do here?' or 'What would a calm parent do?' can guide everyday decisions. It is worth choosing identities that reflect your own values rather than other people's expectations, and holding them flexibly, because people grow and change.
A note of care

Identity can also work against us. Beliefs such as 'I'm bad with money' or 'I'm not a morning person' can become self-fulfilling. Noticing these labels, and asking whether they are facts or habits of thought, is an important part of change. Be gentle here: shifting how you see yourself takes time.

example.title: Illustrative example: 'I'm someone who cooks'
example.text: Ananya, who lived in a hostel and then a shared flat in Bengaluru, had always told friends, 'I can't cook.' After moving out, she wanted to eat better. Instead of setting a goal like 'cook five days a week', she started thinking of herself as 'someone who can make simple meals'. Each time she made poha or dal, she treated it as a small vote for that identity. Months later, cooking felt like part of who she was, not a chore she forced herself to do. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Change happens at the level of outcomes, processes and identity.
Habits tied to identity tend to last longer than habits tied to goals.
Each small action is a vote for the person you want to become.
Notice limiting labels about yourself and question whether they are true.
reflect: Which label about yourself might be holding you back?
What small action today would be a vote for the person you want to be?

lessons.title: Four ways to shape a habit
lessons.idea: The Four Laws of Behavior Change
cards: The book suggests making a good habit obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying.
To break a habit, flip them: make it invisible, unattractive, difficult and unsatisfying.
You don't need all four at once; one adjustment can help.
lessons.tryThis: Choose one habit you want. Write the four laws down: obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying. Next to each, write one small change you could make for this habit, such as placing a cue in sight or pairing it with music you like. Pick the one that seems weakest right now and make that change today.

body.intro: Atomic Habits offers a simple framework for building good habits and breaking bad ones, which the author calls the Four Laws of Behaviour Change. These laws are based on a model of how habits form: a cue, a craving, a response and a reward. This lesson walks through each in plain language. This lesson summarises ideas from Atomic Habits by James Clear in our own words.
sections: The habit loop

The book describes habits as a loop. A cue is something that triggers the behaviour, such as seeing your phone. A craving is the desire for a change in state, such as wanting distraction. The response is the action, such as unlocking the phone. The reward is what you get, such as a moment of entertainment. Over time, the loop runs so quickly that it feels automatic. The four laws map onto these four steps.
Make it obvious

The first law relates to the cue. If you want a habit to happen, make the cue easy to see. Put your running shoes by the door. Keep a book on your pillow. Write a specific plan, such as 'I will meditate for two minutes at 7 a.m. in the bedroom'. The book suggests that many people do not lack motivation so much as clarity about when and where they will act.
Make it attractive

The second law relates to craving. Habits that feel appealing are more likely to happen. One approach the book describes is pairing something you need to do with something you enjoy, for example listening to a favourite podcast only while walking. Another is spending time with people for whom the habit is normal, so it feels like part of fitting in.
Make it easy

The third law relates to the response. The less effort a habit needs, the more likely it is to happen. Reducing steps, such as preparing your gym bag the night before, helps. The book also introduces the Two-Minute Rule: scale a new habit down so it takes about two minutes to start. 'Read before bed' becomes 'read one page'. Once starting is easy, continuing often follows.
Make it satisfying

The fourth law relates to reward. We repeat what feels good. Because many good habits pay off only later, the book suggests adding a small immediate satisfaction, such as ticking off a habit tracker. For breaking bad habits, the laws are inverted: make the cue invisible, the craving unattractive, the action difficult and the result unsatisfying. You do not need to use all four laws at once. Often, improving just the weakest one is enough to tip a habit from 'sometimes' to 'usually'.

example.title: Illustrative example: Vikram's water habit
example.text: Vikram, who works long shifts at a call centre in Gurugram, often went hours without drinking water. Using the four laws, he placed a filled bottle on his desk before each shift (obvious), chose a bottle he liked (attractive), refilled it at a cooler right next to his bay (easy), and marked a tally on a sticky note each time he finished it (satisfying). None of these steps was dramatic, but together they made the habit much more likely. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Habits follow a loop: cue, craving, response, reward.
Make good habits obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying.
The Two-Minute Rule shrinks a new habit so it is easy to start.
To break a habit, invert the laws: invisible, unattractive, difficult, unsatisfying.
reflect: Pick one habit you want. Which of the four laws is weakest for it right now?
What is a two-minute version of a habit you have been putting off?

lessons.title: Attach new habits to old ones
cards: An existing routine can act as a cue for a new one.
The pattern: after I do my current habit, I will do my new habit.
Being specific about when and where makes it easier to follow through.
lessons.tryThis: List five things you already do every day without fail. Choose one as an anchor and write a stack: 'After I [current habit], I will [new habit].' Keep the new habit under two minutes. Stick the sentence somewhere you will see it, such as the fridge or your phone lock screen, and try it for seven days.

body.intro: One of the most practical ideas in Atomic Habits is habit stacking: linking a new habit to one you already do every day. Because your existing routines already happen reliably, they can act as natural reminders for something new. This lesson explains how stacking works and how to use it well. This lesson summarises ideas from Atomic Habits by James Clear in our own words.
sections: Using what already happens

Every day contains dozens of habits you no longer think about: brushing your teeth, making tea, locking the door, sitting down at your desk. These actions happen at fairly predictable times and places. Habit stacking treats each one as a hook. Instead of trying to remember a new habit out of nowhere, you attach it to an old one. The old habit becomes the cue for the new one.
The stacking formula

The book offers a simple sentence pattern: 'After I [current habit], I will [new habit].' For example: 'After I pour my morning tea, I will write one line in my journal.' Or: 'After I sit down for lunch, I will put my phone face down.' Writing the sentence makes the plan concrete. It answers the question of when the habit will happen, which is often what goes missing in vague intentions.
Choosing the right anchor

Not every existing habit makes a good anchor. A good anchor happens at the same frequency you want for the new habit, at a suitable place, and at a moment when you have the time and energy. If you want to stretch daily, attaching it to something you do only on weekends will not work. If you want to read, attaching it to a moment when children are demanding attention may not either. A little thought about timing makes stacking far more reliable.
Building chains

Once one stack is working, you can link more habits onto it, creating a small routine. For instance: after I pour my tea, I will write one line in my journal; after I write my line, I will look at my plan for the day. These chains can turn scattered intentions into a calm, predictable start or end to the day. It is wise to add links slowly, one at a time, so the chain does not become overwhelming.
When stacking does not stick

If a stack keeps failing, the usual reasons are that the anchor is unreliable, the new habit is too big, or the timing is wrong. Rather than blaming yourself, adjust the design: choose a different anchor, shrink the habit, or move it to a calmer moment.

example.title: Illustrative example: the pressure cooker stretch
example.text: Sunita, a homemaker in Lucknow, wanted to stretch every day but kept forgetting. She noticed that every morning she waited a few minutes for the pressure cooker to whistle. She wrote a stack: 'After I put the cooker on the stove, I will do three gentle stretches beside the counter.' The waiting time had always been there; now it had a purpose. Within a few weeks, the stretches felt as automatic as the cooker itself. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Habit stacking links a new habit to an existing daily habit.
Use the formula: 'After I [current habit], I will [new habit].'
Choose anchors with the right timing, place and frequency.
Add links to a chain slowly; adjust the design if a stack fails.
reflect: List three things you do every single day. Which could anchor a new habit?
Which daily waiting moment could hold a small, useful action?

lessons.title: Design your surroundings
lessons.idea: Environment design and the Two-Minute Rule
cards: Your surroundings nudge your choices more than you might notice.
Make cues for good habits visible and remove cues for unwanted ones.
Start a new habit with a version that takes about two minutes, then grow it.
lessons.tryThis: Walk through one room and ask which habits it makes easy. Move one item to support a habit you want, such as a book on the pillow or a water bottle on the desk. Then write the two-minute version of that habit. For one week, do only the two-minute version and stop if you want to.

body.intro: We often assume that people with good habits simply have more willpower. Atomic Habits suggests a different view: people with good habits often have environments that make those habits easier. This lesson explores environment design and the Two-Minute Rule, two tools for making good choices the default. This lesson summarises ideas from Atomic Habits by James Clear in our own words.
sections: Environment shapes behaviour

The book argues that much of our behaviour is a response to our surroundings. If biscuits are on the counter, we eat biscuits. If the TV remote is on the sofa, we watch TV. Small details of where things are placed quietly guide what we do, often without us noticing. This means that changing the environment can be a more reliable way to change behaviour than trying harder.
Designing for good habits

To make a good habit easier, make its cues visible and its tools close at hand. Leave a fruit bowl where you can see it. Keep a water bottle on your desk. Put a guitar on a stand in the living room instead of in a case in a cupboard. The book also suggests creating clear associations between places and activities: one chair for reading, one table for work. When a place is linked to one activity, being there gently prompts it.
The Two-Minute Rule

The Two-Minute Rule says that when you start a new habit, it should take less than two minutes to do. 'Exercise for thirty minutes' becomes 'put on your walking shoes'. 'Study for the exam' becomes 'open your notes'. The idea is to master the habit of showing up before trying to improve it. A habit must be established before it can be improved, and a tiny version is much easier to establish.
Why starting small works

The opening of an activity is often the hardest part. Once your shoes are on, walking for a while feels natural. Once the notebook is open, writing a few lines is easier. The Two-Minute Rule lowers the barrier to starting so that consistency can grow. It is fine to stop after two minutes; the point is to make showing up automatic. Over time, the habit can expand naturally.
Combining both tools

Environment design and the Two-Minute Rule work well together. Arrange your space so the first two minutes of a good habit are effortless, and so the first steps of a bad habit are less convenient. This combination reduces how often you need to rely on willpower at all. A useful exercise is to walk through your home and ask, for each room, which habits it currently makes easy, and whether those are the habits you actually want.

example.title: Illustrative example: the yoga mat by the bed
example.text: Deepak, a teacher in Bhopal, wanted to do morning yoga but rarely managed it. His mat was rolled up behind a cupboard. He moved it to lie open beside his bed every night, and set a two-minute rule: on waking, he only had to sit on the mat and take a few slow breaths. Most mornings, once he was on the mat, he continued for a while longer. Some mornings he stopped at two minutes, and that was fine too. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Surroundings quietly guide behaviour, often more than willpower.
Make cues for good habits visible and tools easy to reach.
The Two-Minute Rule shrinks a new habit so it is easy to start.
Master showing up first; improve the habit later.
reflect: What in your surroundings makes an unwanted habit easy?
What is the two-minute version of a habit you want to build?

lessons.title: Self-sabotage meets a hidden need
lessons.idea: There's no such thing as self-sabotage
cards: Behaviour that holds us back often serves a need we haven't named, such as comfort or safety.
Seeing that need is more useful than blaming yourself.
Once the need is clear, you can look for a healthier way to meet it.
lessons.tryThis: Think of one goal you keep getting in the way of. Write down the behaviour that blocks it. Then ask: 'If this behaviour were protecting me from something, what would it be?' Write whatever comes up without judging it. Finally, write one gentler way to meet that same need. If this stirs heavy feelings, pause and consider support.

body.intro: Self-sabotage is a familiar frustration: we want something, and then we act in ways that push it away. The Mountain Is You offers a striking reframe: self-sabotage is often not irrational at all. It may be a way of meeting a need we have not fully recognised. This lesson explores that idea with care. This lesson summarises ideas from The Mountain Is You by Brianna Wiest in our own words.
sections: What self-sabotage looks like

Self-sabotage can take many forms: procrastinating on an important task, picking fights in a relationship that is going well, overspending right after deciding to save, or staying up late before a big day. From the outside, these look like simple failures of discipline. The book invites us to look more closely at what these behaviours might be doing for us.
A hidden need

The book's central suggestion is that self-sabotaging behaviour often meets an unconscious need. Procrastination might protect us from the fear of being judged. Avoiding a promotion might protect us from the discomfort of more visibility. Clinging to a familiar but unhappy situation might protect us from the uncertainty of change. The behaviour is not random; it is a kind of protection that once made sense, even if it no longer serves us.
Comfort with the familiar

The book also discusses how people tend to feel more comfortable with what is familiar, even if it is not good for them. Change, even positive change, can feel unsafe because it is unknown. When life starts to improve, part of us may try to pull it back to what we are used to. Understanding this can turn frustration into curiosity: 'What part of me feels unsafe with this change?'
Meeting the need differently

Once the need is visible, the question shifts from 'How do I stop this behaviour?' to 'How can I meet this need in a healthier way?' If procrastination protects you from fear of judgement, perhaps you can share early drafts with one trusted person to make judgement feel less threatening. If overspending soothes stress, perhaps there are other ways to soothe yourself. The behaviour often loosens its grip once the underlying need is acknowledged.
When to seek support

Some patterns are deep and connected to painful experiences. If self-sabotage feels overwhelming or tied to difficult memories, speaking with a qualified professional can help. This lesson is for general reflection, not therapy.

example.title: Illustrative example: the unsent application
example.text: Karan, a junior architect in Chandigarh, had wanted to apply for a design fellowship for two years. Each time the deadline approached, he found reasons to delay until it passed. When he reflected honestly, he realised that applying meant risking rejection by people he admired, and not applying protected him from that hurt. Seeing this did not make the fear disappear, but it helped him plan differently: he asked a mentor to review his portfolio early, which made the process feel less lonely. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Self-sabotage often protects us from something we fear.
Ask what need the behaviour is meeting, not only how to stop it.
Familiar situations can feel safer than better but unknown ones.
Meet the underlying need in a healthier way; seek support if patterns feel heavy.
reflect: Think of a time you held yourself back. What might that behaviour have protected you from?
What would it look like to meet that need in a kinder way?

lessons.title: Triggers as signposts
lessons.idea: Your triggers are the guides to your freedom
cards: Strong reactions can point to something that matters to you or still needs care.
Getting curious about a reaction, rather than only reacting, creates room to choose.
A trigger can be information, not just discomfort.
lessons.tryThis: The next time you notice a reaction that feels bigger than the moment, pause for three slow breaths and silently name the feeling. Later, when calm, write three lines: what happened, what it reminded you of, and what you needed. Do this for a few triggers over two weeks and look for patterns. Seek support if it feels overwhelming.

body.intro: A trigger is a moment when a small event provokes a reaction much bigger than the situation seems to call for. A casual comment stings for days, a delayed reply sparks panic, a certain tone of voice makes us shut down. The Mountain Is You suggests that, uncomfortable as they are, triggers can be signposts pointing towards what needs care. This lesson explores how to read them gently. This lesson summarises ideas from The Mountain Is You by Brianna Wiest in our own words.
sections: What a trigger is

Everyday language often uses 'triggered' loosely, but the idea here is specific: a reaction that feels out of proportion to the present moment. If a friend forgetting your birthday leaves you mildly disappointed, that is an ordinary response. If it leaves you feeling worthless for a week, something deeper may be involved. The intensity is the clue. It suggests that the present event has touched an older feeling or belief.
Triggers as information

The book's view is that triggers show us where we have unresolved feelings or unmet needs. Rather than treating them only as problems to avoid, we can treat them as information. A strong reaction to criticism might point to a long-held fear of not being good enough. Strong jealousy might point to something you deeply want but have not allowed yourself to pursue. In this way, the trigger becomes a guide rather than just an enemy.
Pausing before reacting

When a trigger hits, the urge is often to react immediately: to snap back, withdraw, or spiral into worry. A small pause can make a big difference. Taking a few slow breaths, naming the feeling silently ('this is hurt' or 'this is fear'), or stepping away for a moment gives space between the trigger and the response. In that space, you can choose a response that fits your values rather than the old pattern.
Looking underneath

Later, when you are calmer, it can help to reflect: What exactly set this off? What did it remind me of? What did I believe about myself in that moment? Writing the answers down can make patterns clearer over time. You may notice that certain kinds of situations reliably stir the same feelings, and that awareness alone often softens their power.
Gentleness and support

Some triggers are connected to painful past experiences. Exploring them can stir up difficult feelings. Go at your own pace, and if a trigger feels overwhelming or connected to trauma, a qualified professional can help you work through it safely. Self-reflection is useful, but it is not a substitute for care when you need it.

example.title: Illustrative example: the 'seen' message
example.text: Nisha, a marketing executive in Mumbai, noticed that when friends saw her messages without replying, she felt a wave of panic and spent hours rereading what she had written. One evening, instead of spiralling, she paused and wrote down what she felt: 'I'm afraid they're annoyed with me and will leave.' She realised this fear was familiar from school years when she often felt left out. Naming it did not erase it, but the next time it happened, she recognised the old feeling and reminded herself that a late reply usually just means a busy friend. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: A trigger is a reaction that feels bigger than the present moment calls for.
The intensity of a reaction can point to older feelings or needs.
Pause, breathe and name the feeling before responding.
Reflect later on patterns; seek professional support if triggers feel overwhelming.
reflect: What situation reliably produces a stronger reaction in you than you would like?
If that reaction could speak, what might it be trying to protect?

lessons.title: Building emotional intelligence
cards: Emotional intelligence includes noticing, naming and understanding your feelings.
Feelings carry useful messages, even uncomfortable ones.
Understanding your own emotions helps in understanding others too.
lessons.tryThis: Set three gentle reminders on your phone for tomorrow. Each time one goes off, pause and ask: 'What am I feeling right now, and where do I notice it in my body?' Try to name the feeling with a precise word rather than 'fine' or 'bad'. In the evening, look at the three words and notice what they tell you.

body.intro: Emotional intelligence is the ability to notice, understand and work with emotions, both your own and other people's. The Mountain Is You treats building emotional intelligence as a key part of moving past self-sabotage. This lesson explores what that looks like in daily life, in plain language. This lesson summarises ideas from The Mountain Is You by Brianna Wiest in our own words.
sections: Feelings are not the enemy

Many of us grow up learning, directly or indirectly, that certain feelings are bad: anger is rude, sadness is weakness, fear is shameful. As a result, we may push feelings away or pretend they are not there. The book suggests that emotions carry useful information about our needs and boundaries. Anger can signal that a line has been crossed. Sadness can signal loss. Anxiety can signal that something matters to us. Ignoring them does not make them go away; it often makes them louder.
Feeling without being ruled

Emotional intelligence does not mean suppressing feelings, and it does not mean acting on every feeling either. It means allowing yourself to feel something fully while still choosing how to respond. You can feel angry and decide not to shout. You can feel afraid and still take a careful step forward. Learning to hold a feeling without being swept away by it is a skill that develops with practice.
Naming emotions

A simple but powerful habit is putting feelings into words. 'I feel bad' is vague. 'I feel disappointed and a bit embarrassed' is much clearer. A richer vocabulary for emotions makes it easier to understand what you need. Some people find it helpful to check in with themselves a few times a day: What am I feeling right now? Where do I notice it in my body?
Understanding others

Emotional intelligence also includes noticing what others may be feeling. A colleague who snaps might be under pressure. A friend who goes quiet might be hurting. Being curious instead of assuming the worst, and asking gently ('You seem a bit low today, is everything okay?'), can strengthen relationships and reduce conflict.
Practising patience with yourself

Building emotional intelligence is a gradual process, and everyone has days when old reactions take over. That is part of learning. Each time you notice a feeling, name it, or pause before reacting, you are strengthening the skill, even if the next moment does not go perfectly.

example.title: Illustrative example: the tense dinner
example.text: At a family dinner in Patna, Aditya's father criticised his choice of career in front of relatives. Aditya felt his face go hot and wanted to argue loudly. Instead, he took a breath and silently named what he felt: 'hurt and embarrassed'. He said calmly, 'I'd like to talk about this later, just us two.' Later that evening, they spoke privately, and Aditya was able to explain his plans without the heat of the moment. The feeling had not vanished, but he had chosen how to respond. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Emotions carry useful information about needs and boundaries.
Emotional intelligence means feeling fully while choosing how to respond.
Naming emotions precisely makes them easier to understand.
Curiosity about others' feelings can strengthen relationships.
reflect: Which emotion do you find hardest to allow yourself to feel?
When did you last respond to a strong feeling in a way you were proud of?

lessons.title: Acting as your future self
cards: Change becomes real through small actions, not only insight.
Imagining the person you want to become can guide everyday choices.
Progress can feel uncomfortable because it is unfamiliar, not because it is wrong.
lessons.tryThis: Write a short paragraph describing an ordinary day in the life of the person you hope to become in a year. Underline one habit in that paragraph. Tomorrow, do a tiny version of that habit, even if you do not feel ready. Each evening this week, ask, 'What would my future self do with thirty spare minutes?'

body.intro: It is easy to imagine a better future and much harder to live in a way that leads there. The Mountain Is You ends by encouraging readers to start building a new future through small, deliberate choices today, guided by the person they want to become. This lesson explores how that idea can work in everyday life. This lesson summarises ideas from The Mountain Is You by Brianna Wiest in our own words.
sections: Imagining your future self

The book invites readers to picture the person they hope to become: how they spend their days, how they treat themselves and others, what they value. This is not about fantasy or perfection. It is about getting clear enough on a direction that daily choices can be measured against it. A clear picture makes it easier to notice when you are drifting away from it.
Acting before you feel ready

A common trap is waiting to feel confident, motivated or ready before acting. The book suggests that these feelings often come after action, not before. If you wait to feel like a disciplined person before acting like one, you may wait a long time. Taking small actions consistent with your future self, even when you do not feel ready, can gradually build the confidence you were waiting for.
Letting go of the old self

Moving towards a new future can involve grief for the old one. Familiar habits, relationships or self-images may no longer fit. The book acknowledges that this can feel uncomfortable and even lonely. It is normal to feel a pull back towards the old patterns. Recognising that discomfort as part of growth, rather than as a sign that something is wrong, can make it easier to keep going.
Daily choices as building blocks

The future is built mostly from ordinary days. How you start the morning, how you respond to stress, what you do with free time: these small choices add up. Asking 'What would my future self do here?' at a few key moments each day can gently steer your path. You do not need to get every choice right. You just need to keep returning to the direction you chose.
Meaning and purpose

Building a future is not only about productivity or achievement. The book connects it to living in line with your values and finding meaning. A future self might be calmer, kinder, more present with family, or more creative, not only more successful. Choosing what matters to you, rather than what others expect, makes the journey more worthwhile.

example.title: Illustrative example: the future-self question
example.text: Shreya, a mid-career accountant in Coimbatore, often imagined herself as someone who painted again, as she had in college. She kept waiting for a free month that never came. She started asking herself each evening, 'What would the painter version of me do with thirty spare minutes?' Some evenings the answer was 'sketch for ten minutes'. Over a few months, she had filled a sketchbook and felt more like herself than she had in years. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Picture the person you want to become as a guide for daily choices.
Confidence often follows action, not the other way round.
Letting go of old patterns can feel uncomfortable; that is part of growth.
Build the future through ordinary daily choices aligned with your values.
reflect: Describe one day in the life of the person you hope to become.
What is one small action that version of you would take tomorrow?

lessons.title: Know how you respond to expectations
cards: The book describes four tendencies: Upholder, Questioner, Obliger and Rebel.
They differ in how people respond to expectations from others and from themselves.
Knowing your tendency helps you choose habit strategies that suit you.
lessons.tryThis: Think about two promises: one you made to someone else and one you made to yourself. Which did you keep more easily? Use that clue to guess which tendency might fit you. Then redesign one stalled habit to suit it, for example by adding a reason, a partner or a sense of choice. Try it for one week.

body.intro: Why do some people keep every promise to others but struggle with promises to themselves? Why do some resist any rule they are given? Better Than Before introduces a framework called the Four Tendencies, which describes how people respond to expectations. This lesson explains the framework and how it can help you design habits that suit you. This lesson summarises ideas from Better Than Before by Gretchen Rubin in our own words.
sections: Two kinds of expectations

The framework starts with two kinds of expectations. Outer expectations come from others: a work deadline, a request from a friend, a doctor's suggestion. Inner expectations come from yourself: a resolution to read more, a plan to start exercising. The book observes that people differ in how they respond to each kind, and that this difference shapes how habits work for them.
The four tendencies

The book describes four patterns. Upholders tend to meet both outer and inner expectations readily; they like rules and plans. Questioners tend to meet expectations only when they understand and agree with the reasons; they turn outer expectations into inner ones. Obligers tend to meet outer expectations reliably but struggle with inner ones; they keep promises to others more easily than to themselves. Rebels tend to resist expectations of both kinds and prefer to act from choice and freedom.
Why this matters for habits

Because people respond differently, the same habit strategy will not suit everyone. An Upholder may do well with a simple schedule. A Questioner may need to research why a habit is worthwhile before committing. An Obliger may benefit most from outer accountability, such as a walking partner or a class. A Rebel may do better framing a habit as a choice that expresses who they are, rather than a rule they must obey.
Using the framework wisely

The tendencies are a tool for self-understanding, not a fixed label or a personality test with a score. Many people recognise themselves strongly in one, while others see a mix. The value lies in asking: 'What kind of approach actually works for me?' rather than copying someone else's routine and feeling like a failure when it does not fit.
Understanding others

The framework can also help in relationships and at work. If a colleague keeps asking 'why', they may simply need reasons, not be difficult. If a family member resists being told what to do, offering choices may work better than instructions. Seeing these differences can reduce frustration on both sides.

example.title: Illustrative example: the yoga class
example.text: Divya, an IT professional in Noida, had tried many times to do yoga at home using videos and always stopped after a few days. When she read about the Four Tendencies, she recognised herself as likely an Obliger: she never missed a meeting at work, but her own plans slipped. She joined a small morning class where the teacher expected her, and a friend came along too. With outer accountability in place, she attended regularly for months. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: People respond differently to outer and inner expectations.
The four patterns are Upholder, Questioner, Obliger and Rebel.
Choose habit strategies that suit how you respond to expectations.
Use the framework for understanding, not as a fixed label.
reflect: Do you find it easier to keep promises to others or to yourself?
Which habit strategy has failed for you, and might it have suited a different tendency?

lessons.title: Strengthen the foundation
cards: Some habits support many others, such as sleep, movement, eating well and decluttering.
When these basics slip, other habits tend to wobble too.
Starting with a foundation habit can make the rest easier.
lessons.tryThis: Pick one foundation: sleep, movement, food and drink, or order. Choose one small step for it, such as phone out of the bedroom by a set time, a ten-minute walk, a glass of water with each meal, or a two-minute evening tidy. Do it for seven days and notice whether any other part of life feels easier.

body.intro: When life feels chaotic, it can be hard to change anything. Better Than Before describes a Strategy of Foundation: focusing first on habits that strengthen self-command and make everything else easier. This lesson explores what foundation habits are and why they deserve attention. This lesson summarises ideas from Better Than Before by Gretchen Rubin in our own words.
sections: What foundation habits are

The book identifies certain areas that tend to support all other habits. Broadly, these are sleeping, moving, eating and drinking wisely, and keeping your surroundings in order. When these areas are neglected, people often feel tired, irritable or scattered, and other habits become much harder to keep. When they are reasonably steady, there is more energy and patience available for everything else. The book's idea is that strengthening these foundations first can make later changes feel less like a struggle.
Sleep

Sleep is often the first thing sacrificed when time is short. Yet tiredness can make it harder to resist temptation, focus or stay patient. Small steps, such as going to bed a little earlier or keeping screens out of bed, can make a noticeable difference for many people. Everyone's sleep needs differ; if you have persistent sleep problems, a qualified professional can help.
Movement

Movement does not have to mean intense exercise. Walking, stretching, climbing stairs or dancing in the kitchen all count. Many people find that some daily movement lifts their mood and energy. The aim is regular, enjoyable movement that suits your body and life, not a punishing routine.
Eating and drinking

Eating regular meals and drinking enough water can steady energy across the day. The book's interest here is not in a particular diet but in avoiding the energy crashes and irritability that can come from skipping meals or relying heavily on quick snacks. This lesson does not offer dietary advice; for specific needs, consult a qualified professional.
Order in your surroundings

A cluttered, chaotic space can make it harder to think clearly. The book suggests that bringing some outer order, such as making the bed or clearing a desk, can contribute to a sense of inner calm. It does not have to be perfect; even small areas of order can help. Together, these four foundations create a base on which other habits can grow more easily.

example.title: Illustrative example: fixing sleep first
example.text: Ravi, a sales manager in Hyderabad, wanted to start studying for a certification, exercise more and spend more time with his kids. He kept failing at all three. Looking at his days, he realised he was sleeping only a few hours most nights because he scrolled his phone until late. He decided to work on just one thing first: phone off and charging outside the bedroom by eleven. After a few weeks of better rest, he found it much easier to wake up for a morning walk and stay patient in the evenings. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Foundation habits support all other habits.
The foundations are sleep, movement, eating and drinking wisely, and outer order.
Strengthening one foundation can make other changes easier.
This is general learning; consult a professional for health-specific needs.
reflect: Which foundation, sleep, movement, food or order, feels weakest for you right now?
How might improving it make another habit easier?

lessons.title: What you track, you notice
cards: Keeping track of an action makes it more visible.
Simple monitoring, like noting spending or steps, often changes behaviour on its own.
Track without judging; the aim is awareness.
lessons.tryThis: Choose one behaviour you suspect you underestimate, such as screen time, snacks or small spends. Track it for seven days using the simplest method available, such as a note on your phone or a built-in report. Do not try to change it yet. At the end of the week, write one sentence about what surprised you. This is not financial advice.

body.intro: It is surprisingly hard to change something you are not paying attention to. Better Than Before describes the Strategy of Monitoring: keeping track of a behaviour so that you see it clearly. This lesson explores why simply noticing can shift habits, and how to monitor without becoming obsessive. Where money is mentioned, this is general learning only, not financial advice. This lesson summarises ideas from Better Than Before by Gretchen Rubin in our own words.
sections: We underestimate what we do not track

Many people, if asked how much time they spend on their phone, how much they spend on snacks, or how many steps they walk, give answers that turn out to be quite far from reality once they actually measure. The book points out that our impressions of our own behaviour are often unreliable. Monitoring replaces guesswork with information, which makes it easier to decide what, if anything, to change.
Noticing changes behaviour

Simply tracking something can nudge it in a better direction. When you write down every purchase, you may pause before an impulse buy because you know you will have to record it. When you note what you eat, you may become more aware of mindless snacking. Monitoring creates a moment of attention, and attention gives you a chance to choose.
What to monitor

It helps to monitor only what matters to you right now, rather than tracking everything. Choose one or two behaviours connected to a habit you want to change: hours of sleep, minutes of movement, money spent on eating out, or time on social media. Keep the method simple: a notebook, a note on your phone, or a built-in screen-time report. The easier it is, the more likely you are to keep it up.
Monitoring money

Money is one area where monitoring often brings clarity. Looking back at a month of UPI payments or card statements and grouping them into a few categories can reveal surprising patterns. The aim is awareness, not judgement. Any decisions about budgeting, saving or investing depend on your own circumstances, and a qualified professional can help with larger choices. This is not financial advice.
Avoiding the trap of over-tracking

Monitoring can become counterproductive if it turns into anxiety or perfectionism. If tracking makes you feel worse rather than more aware, simplify it, track less often, or pause it altogether. The goal is useful information, not constant self-surveillance. It is fine to monitor for a few weeks to learn, then stop once the habit is steady.

example.title: Illustrative example: the screen-time surprise
example.text: Meenakshi, a schoolteacher in Madurai, felt she used her phone 'only a little' in the evenings. Out of curiosity, she checked her phone's built-in screen-time report for a week. The total was much higher than she expected, mostly short-video apps after dinner. She did not set strict limits; she simply looked at the report each Sunday. Over a month, her evening use dropped as she became more aware, and she started reading with her daughter instead. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Our impressions of our own behaviour are often inaccurate.
Tracking creates a moment of attention that can shift behaviour.
Monitor one or two things that matter, using a simple method.
Stop or simplify if tracking causes anxiety. Not financial advice.
reflect: Which behaviour do you suspect you underestimate?
What is the simplest way you could track it for one week?

lessons.title: Abstainer or moderator?
cards: Some people find it easier to avoid a temptation completely (abstainers).
Others do better with a little, now and then (moderators).
Neither is better; knowing which fits you helps you set useful rules.
lessons.tryThis: Pick one tempting thing you would like to have less of. For one week, try the Abstainer approach: none at all. For the following week, try the Moderator approach: a small, planned amount. At the end, compare how each felt. Which brought calm, and which brought bargaining? Use that to choose your approach.

body.intro: When trying to cut back on something tempting, some people do best by giving it up entirely, while others do best by allowing a little. Better Than Before calls these two styles Abstainers and Moderators. This lesson explains both and how knowing your style can make habits easier. This lesson summarises ideas from Better Than Before by Gretchen Rubin in our own words.
sections: Two ways of handling temptation

The book observes that people respond to temptation in different ways. Abstainers find it easier to have none of something than a little. Once they start, they find it hard to stop, and constant decisions about 'how much' wear them out. Moderators find that strict rules make them feel deprived and rebellious; having a little now and then satisfies them and helps them stay on track.
The Abstainer's experience

For an Abstainer, a rule like 'no sweets on weekdays' can actually feel freeing. Instead of debating every time sweets appear, the answer is simply no. The book suggests that Abstainers often feel relief rather than deprivation once they decide firmly. Trying to moderate, by contrast, can lead to endless bargaining: 'Just one more. Well, it's already open. I'll start tomorrow.'
The Moderator's experience

For a Moderator, the same strict rule might make sweets seem even more desirable. Knowing they can have a small piece after dinner makes it easier to skip the rest. Moderators tend to do well with flexibility, and an absolute ban can backfire, leading to overindulgence once the rule is broken.
Finding your style

To discover your style, think about past experiences. When you tried to cut back on something, did having a little satisfy you, or did it open the door to having a lot? Did a firm 'never' feel like relief or like a cage? Your style might differ between areas of life; you might be an Abstainer with chips but a Moderator with television. The book stresses that neither style is better; they are just different. You might also notice that your style shifts with stress or tiredness, which is another useful thing to learn about yourself.
Respecting others' styles

Knowing about these two styles can also reduce friction with family and friends. An Abstainer may not want a 'tiny taste' offered repeatedly. A Moderator may resent being told to give something up entirely. Respecting each person's approach makes support more effective.

example.title: Illustrative example: the namkeen packet
example.text: Gaurav, a bank clerk in Kanpur, loved salty namkeen. He kept trying to eat 'just a handful' in the evenings, but often finished the whole packet. When he read about Abstainers and Moderators, he recognised that he was probably an Abstainer for this snack. He stopped buying it for home and kept it only for festivals. To his surprise, he felt calmer, not deprived, because he was no longer negotiating with himself every night. His wife, a Moderator, kept enjoying a small bowl now and then. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Abstainers find it easier to have none than a little.
Moderators find that a little now and then keeps them on track.
Neither style is better; find out which suits you in each area.
Respect others' styles when offering support.
reflect: When you allow yourself a little of something tempting, what usually happens next?
Is there an area where a firm rule might actually feel like relief?

lessons.title: Spot your loopholes
cards: We often invent reasons to skip a habit 'just this once'.
Common examples include 'it's a special occasion' or 'I'll make up for it tomorrow'.
Naming the loophole in advance makes it easier to notice in the moment.
lessons.tryThis: For the next few days, keep a short list of the excuses you hear yourself making to skip a habit. Next to each, write which type of loophole it might be, such as tomorrow logic or 'this doesn't count'. Then choose one upcoming occasion, like a festival or trip, and decide calmly in advance how you will handle it.

body.intro: We are remarkably creative at finding reasons to skip our own habits. Better Than Before describes the Strategy of Loophole-Spotting: learning to recognise the excuses we make, so we can catch them in the moment. This lesson walks through common loopholes and how to respond. Where money is mentioned, this is general learning only, not financial advice. This lesson summarises ideas from Better Than Before by Gretchen Rubin in our own words.
sections: What a loophole is

A loophole is a justification that lets us off the hook from a habit we have chosen. It often sounds reasonable in the moment. 'I've been so good all week, I deserve this.' 'It's a special occasion.' 'I'll start fresh on Monday.' The book suggests that by naming common types of loopholes, we can spot them more easily and decide whether we really want to use them.
Common types

The book lists several categories. Moral licensing: I've been good, so I've earned a reward that undoes my effort. Tomorrow logic: it's fine to skip today because I'll do it tomorrow. Lack of control: I had no choice. Planning to fail: putting yourself in a tempting situation 'by accident'. This doesn't count: holidays, weekends or travel somehow don't count. Questionable assumption: 'I'm too busy'. Concern for others: 'I don't want to be rude by refusing'. Fake self-actualisation: 'You only live once'. One-coin loophole: 'one time won't matter'.
Catching loopholes in action

Spotting a loophole does not mean you must never use it. It means you notice when you are reaching for one and make a conscious choice. Some people find it helpful to say the loophole out loud or write it down: 'I'm using tomorrow logic.' Naming it often takes away some of its persuasive power. Sometimes you will decide the exception is worth it; that is your choice to make.
Planning for predictable exceptions

Many loopholes appear at predictable times: weddings, festivals, travel, exam weeks. Instead of pretending these will not happen, you can plan for them. Decide in advance how you want to handle Diwali sweets, a family wedding, or a work trip. A planned exception is different from a loophole because you chose it calmly, not in the heat of the moment.
Loopholes and money

Loopholes are common in spending too: 'It's on sale, so I'm saving money', or 'It's only a small amount'. Noticing these thoughts can help you decide more deliberately. What counts as reasonable spending depends on your own situation. This is not financial advice.

example.title: Illustrative example: the 'it's a sale' loophole
example.text: Tanvi, a young professional in Pune, wanted to cut back on online clothes shopping. During a big online sale, she found herself thinking, 'If I buy now, I'm actually saving money.' She recognised this as a loophole she had used many times. She paused, wrote it in her notes app, and asked whether she would buy the item at full price. The answer was no, so she closed the app. She did buy one thing she had planned for months, which felt like a choice rather than a slip. This is an illustrative story and not financial advice.

takeaways: Loopholes are justifications that let us skip our own habits.
Common types include moral licensing, tomorrow logic and 'this doesn't count'.
Naming a loophole helps you choose deliberately.
Plan for predictable exceptions in advance. Not financial advice.
reflect: Which loophole do you use most often?
What predictable occasion coming up could you plan for now?

lessons.title: Mind and body are connected
cards: The book explores how very difficult experiences can affect the body as well as the mind.
It suggests that stress can be felt physically, not only as thoughts.
Understanding this connection can make reactions feel less confusing.
lessons.tryThis: This is optional and only if it feels comfortable. During an ordinary, calm moment today, pause and gently notice your shoulders, jaw and breathing for about thirty seconds, without trying to change anything. If this brings up anything distressing, stop and do something grounding instead, such as looking around the room. Consider reaching out to a qualified professional if difficult feelings arise.

body.intro: The Body Keeps the Score is a widely read book about trauma, written by a psychiatrist who has worked with trauma survivors for many years. Its central idea is that overwhelming experiences can affect not only how we think and feel, but also how our bodies respond. This lesson introduces that idea gently and in general terms. This lesson summarises ideas from The Body Keeps the Score by Bessel van der Kolk in our own words. It is for general understanding only and is not therapy, diagnosis or treatment advice. If this topic brings up difficult feelings, please consider speaking with a qualified professional.
