Having read about power tactics, she recognised the pattern. She did not become cold or suspicious of everyone; she simply made decisions using the same fair criteria for all team members, and responded to praise with a polite thank-you. The pattern lost its effect. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: The book catalogues historical power tactics, many of them manipulative.
Reading for awareness helps you recognise power games around you.
Knowing a tactic does not mean using it; ethics and trust matter.
Use awareness to protect yourself and seek help when pressure is serious.
reflect: Can you recall a situation where someone used flattery or guilt to influence you?
Which of your values would guide your response if it happened again?

lessons.title: Pause before you speak
lessons.idea: Law 4: Always Say Less Than Necessary
cards: The book argues that saying more than needed can weaken your position.
A wellness-friendly reading: you don't owe everyone every detail.
Speaking thoughtfully is a way of keeping healthy boundaries.
lessons.tryThis: In your next meeting or important conversation, make a point of pausing for a breath before you respond. Aim to make one or two clear points instead of many. If someone falls silent after a request, notice the urge to fill the gap, and instead calmly ask a question or take time to think.

body.intro: One of the laws in The 48 Laws of Power advises saying less than necessary. In the book, this is framed as a way to appear powerful and mysterious. Through an awareness lens, there is a more ethical lesson inside it: the value of pausing, listening and choosing words carefully. This lesson explores that gentler version. This lesson summarises ideas from The 48 Laws of Power by Robert Greene in our own words. It is presented for awareness, to help you recognise power dynamics, not as advice to manipulate or deceive anyone.
sections: What the law describes

The book's fourth law suggests that people who talk too much reveal more than they intend, make careless statements and lose credibility, while those who speak less can seem more thoughtful and in control. Its historical examples show figures who used silence and brevity to unsettle others or keep their intentions hidden.
The awareness angle

It helps to recognise when someone is using silence strategically, for example to make you fill the gap with concessions in a negotiation, or to appear more authoritative. If you notice this, you do not have to rush to fill the silence. You can wait, ask a clarifying question, or take time to think. Simply recognising the tactic reduces its pressure.
An ethical version: pause before speaking

Without the manipulation, there is real value in speaking thoughtfully. Pausing before responding, especially when emotions are high, can prevent hurtful words and regretted promises. Listening more than speaking helps you understand others. Saying what you mean clearly and briefly can make communication more respectful of everyone's time. Thoughtful speech also includes knowing when to share. Keeping a friend's confidence, or not spreading gossip at work, is a form of restraint that builds trust rather than mystery.
Not silence as a weapon

There is a difference between thoughtful restraint and using silence to control or punish. Stonewalling a partner, deliberately withholding information that others need, or staying silent to make someone anxious can damage trust. The ethical version of this law is about care in speaking, not about leaving others in the dark.
At work

In meetings, people often feel pressure to say something, anything, to seem engaged. Making one or two considered points can be more useful than many rushed ones. When asked for a commitment, it is fine to say, 'Let me check and get back to you,' rather than promising more than you can deliver.

example.title: Illustrative example: the quiet negotiation
example.text: During a salary discussion in Bengaluru, Pranav's manager offered a figure and then stayed silent. Pranav felt the urge to say 'Okay, that's fine' just to end the awkward pause. Remembering what he had read, he recognised the silence might be applying pressure. He took a breath and said calmly, 'Thank you. I'd like a day to think it over.' The next day, he came back with a clear, honest response. This is an illustrative story and not career or financial advice.

takeaways: The book's law suggests speaking less to appear powerful.
Recognise when silence is being used to pressure you, and take your time.
The ethical lesson is to pause, listen and speak thoughtfully.
Avoid using silence to control or punish others.
reflect: When have you said more than you intended, and why?
In what situation would a short pause help you respond more wisely?

lessons.title: Notice the company you keep
lessons.idea: Law 10: Avoid the unhappy and unlucky
cards: The book warns that other people's moods and habits can spread to us.
This isn't about judging people who are struggling; it's about noticing your own limits.
You can care for others while still protecting your energy.
lessons.tryThis: Over the next week, after spending time with different people, jot down one word for how you feel: energised, calm, drained or anxious. Look for patterns. If one relationship regularly leaves you depleted, think of one kind, clear boundary you could set, and practise saying it aloud before you use it.

body.intro: The 48 Laws of Power includes a law about avoiding people it describes as 'unhappy and unlucky', suggesting that their misfortune can spread. Read literally, this can sound harsh: should we abandon friends who are struggling? Through an awareness lens, there is a more balanced question underneath: how do the people around us affect our wellbeing, and how do we set healthy boundaries without abandoning compassion? This lesson summarises ideas from The 48 Laws of Power by Robert Greene in our own words. It is presented for awareness, to help you recognise power dynamics, not as advice to manipulate or deceive anyone.
sections: What the law describes

The book's tenth law warns that some people bring chaos and negativity wherever they go, and that spending time with them can drag you into their problems. Its historical examples show figures whose association with troublesome individuals led to their downfall. The book's advice is to avoid such people.
Why this needs care

Taken at face value, this law could encourage cutting off anyone going through a hard time, which would be unkind and isolating for them. Everyone experiences difficult periods, illness, loss or bad luck. Abandoning people when they struggle damages trust and community, and we may need the same support ourselves one day.
A balanced reading

A more balanced lesson is that the people we spend time with do influence our mood, habits and outlook. There is a difference between someone going through a hard time and someone who repeatedly creates drama, disrespects boundaries, or pulls others into harmful patterns. Noticing how you feel after spending time with someone, energised, calm, drained or anxious, can be useful information. It can also help to notice your own influence: whether you bring calm or tension to the people around you.
Healthy boundaries

Setting boundaries does not have to mean ending a relationship. It might mean limiting how often you discuss certain topics, not lending money you cannot afford to lose, saying no to plans that leave you depleted, or encouraging a friend to seek professional support instead of becoming their only source of help. Boundaries protect both your wellbeing and the relationship.
Supporting without sinking

You can care for someone who is struggling while also caring for yourself. Listening, checking in and helping them find resources are kind. Taking on their problems as your own, at the cost of your health, is not sustainable.

example.title: Illustrative example: the friend in crisis
example.text: Ayesha's close friend in Lucknow was going through a painful divorce and called her every night for hours. Ayesha wanted to support her but was exhausted and falling behind at work. Rather than pulling away, she said kindly, 'I care about you and want to help. I can talk for half an hour most evenings, and I think a counsellor could also help you through this.' Her friend was hurt at first but later agreed that the extra support made a difference. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: The book's law advises avoiding 'unhappy and unlucky' people; read literally, this can be unkind.
People around us influence our mood and habits.
Distinguish between someone struggling and someone repeatedly harmful.
Set boundaries that protect your wellbeing while keeping compassion.
reflect: How do you usually feel after time with the people closest to you?
Is there a relationship where a gentle boundary would help both of you?

lessons.title: Think to the end
lessons.idea: Law 29: Plan All the Way to the End
cards: The book stresses thinking through where a plan leads before starting.
Considering the likely ending helps you avoid being swept along by short-term wins.
Used ethically, it's simply careful planning.
lessons.tryThis: Choose one decision you are currently facing. Write three questions: What could go wrong? What will this look like in a year? Who else does this affect? Answer each briefly. Then set one first step and one date to check in and adjust. Keep the planning to a single page so it leads to action.

body.intro: Another law in The 48 Laws of Power advises planning all the way to the end. In the book, this is about anticipating every move to secure power. Separated from its power-seeking frame, it carries a useful everyday lesson: think through consequences before acting. This lesson explores that idea ethically. This lesson summarises ideas from The 48 Laws of Power by Robert Greene in our own words. It is presented for awareness, to help you recognise power dynamics, not as advice to manipulate or deceive anyone.
sections: What the law describes

The book's twenty-ninth law argues that many people fail because they focus on immediate gains and do not think through what will happen next. Its historical examples show figures who succeeded early but were undone by consequences they had not anticipated, and others who planned carefully and adapted as events unfolded.
The awareness angle

Recognising this law can help you notice when others are planning several steps ahead, for instance offering a small favour now to secure a larger request later. Awareness allows you to ask, 'Where might this lead?' before agreeing to something, and to set clear terms.
Ethical planning: think to the end

Planning ahead in an ethical way means considering how decisions will affect you and others over time. Before starting a project, changing jobs or making a commitment, asking 'What could go wrong? What will this look like in a year? Who else does this affect?' can prevent avoidable problems. It also helps you prepare for obstacles rather than being caught off guard. Writing down the main risks and a simple response for each can make big decisions feel less frightening, because you have already thought about what you would do.
Plans need flexibility

The book also stresses adapting plans as circumstances change. Real life rarely follows a script. Good planning includes considering a few scenarios, building in some slack, and being willing to adjust. Rigid plans can break; flexible ones bend.
Avoiding overplanning

There is a balance. Endless planning can become a way to avoid starting, and trying to control every outcome can cause anxiety. A reasonable plan, followed by action and regular check-ins, is usually more effective than a perfect plan that never begins. A simple rule of thumb is to plan enough to feel prepared, then begin, and review the plan after the first few steps when you have real information to work with.

example.title: Illustrative example: the café idea
example.text: Rohan, a hotel management graduate in Goa, wanted to open a small café. His first impulse was to rent a space immediately. A mentor encouraged him to think it through: What happens in the quiet monsoon months? What if suppliers are late? How long could he manage before the café covers costs? Thinking to the end did not kill the dream; it led him to start with a weekend stall to test demand first. This is an illustrative story and not business or financial advice.

takeaways: The book's law advises planning for consequences far ahead.
Awareness helps you notice when others are planning several steps ahead.
Ethical planning considers effects on you and others over time.
Plans need flexibility; avoid overplanning as a way to delay action.
reflect: Which decision in your life would benefit from thinking 'to the end'?
Do you tend to underplan or overplan? What would a balanced approach look like?

lessons.title: This moment is where life happens
cards: The book's central idea is that life only ever happens now.
Much stress, it suggests, comes from living in thoughts about the past or future.
Bringing attention back to now is something you can practise anytime.
lessons.tryThis: Choose one routine activity tomorrow, such as drinking tea, brushing your teeth or walking to the bus. For the first minute of it, put your phone away and notice what you can see, hear, smell and feel. When your mind wanders, gently bring it back. Do this once a day for a week.

body.intro: Much of our mental life is spent somewhere other than here and now: replaying yesterday's conversation, worrying about next week, planning, regretting, imagining. The Power of Now invites readers to notice how rarely they are fully present, and suggests that life is only ever lived in this moment. This lesson explores that idea in practical terms. This lesson summarises ideas from The Power of Now by Eckhart Tolle in our own words. It is reflective practice, not a treatment for anxiety or any condition.
sections: Living in the mind's timeline

The book observes that the mind tends to move constantly between past and future. We relive old hurts or rehearse future scenarios, often with anxiety or regret. While some planning and reflection are useful, the book suggests that much of this mental movement is habitual and adds unnecessary suffering. We can spend a whole meal thinking about work and barely taste the food.
The present moment

The book's central idea is that the present moment is the only place where life actually happens. The past exists as memory and the future as imagination, both experienced now. Bringing attention to the present, to what you can see, hear and feel right now, can create a sense of spaciousness and calm. This is not about ignoring the future, but about not living entirely inside thoughts about it.
Practical presence

Presence can be practised in ordinary activities. When drinking tea, notice its warmth and taste. When walking, feel your feet on the ground. When someone speaks to you, listen fully instead of preparing your reply. These small moments of attention are a simple way to experience what the book describes. They need no special setting or equipment. Some people like to choose one 'presence cue' for the day, such as every time they open a door, as a reminder to take one conscious breath.
Planning without worrying

The book distinguishes between using time practically, such as making plans, and being psychologically lost in time, such as constant worry about outcomes. You can make a plan and then return your attention to the step in front of you. This allows you to prepare for the future without letting it dominate your present.
Gentleness with the wandering mind

Minds wander; that is normal. Presence is not about forcing out every thought. It is about noticing when you have drifted and gently returning. Each return is a moment of practice, not a failure. If worry or low mood feels persistent or overwhelming, a qualified professional can help; reflective practice is not a substitute for care.

example.title: Illustrative example: the morning chai
example.text: Every morning, Lata in Varanasi drank her chai while scrolling news and thinking about her to-do list. One day she decided to drink the first few sips without her phone, sitting by the window. She noticed the steam, the cardamom smell and the sound of the street waking up. It took only a minute or two, but she felt calmer starting the day. She made it a small daily ritual. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: The mind often lives in past and future rather than the present.
The book suggests life happens only in the present moment.
Presence can be practised in ordinary activities like eating and walking.
Use time practically for planning, then return to the present step.
reflect: Where does your mind usually go when you are doing routine tasks?
Which daily activity could become a small moment of presence?

lessons.title: You can watch your thoughts
cards: The book invites you to notice thoughts as they arise, as if listening to them.
Observing thoughts can create a small gap between you and them.
In that gap, the book describes a sense of calm presence.
lessons.tryThis: Sit quietly for two minutes with a timer. Each time a thought appears, label it with a single word, such as 'planning', 'worrying' or 'remembering', and let it pass without following it. When the timer ends, notice how you feel. Try this once a day for a week. Stop if it feels uncomfortable.

body.intro: Most of us identify closely with our thoughts. If the mind says 'I'm a failure', it feels like the truth. The Power of Now suggests that you can step back and observe your thoughts, and that you are not the same as the stream of thinking in your head. This lesson explores the practice of watching the mind. This lesson summarises ideas from The Power of Now by Eckhart Tolle in our own words. It is reflective practice, not a treatment for anxiety or any condition.
sections: The voice in the head

The book describes the constant inner commentary many people experience: judging, comparing, worrying, planning, replaying. This voice often runs without pause and can feel like it is 'me'. The book suggests that identifying completely with this voice is a major source of unhappiness, because the voice is often repetitive and negative.
Becoming the observer

A key practice in the book is to watch your thoughts as if you were an observer. Instead of being carried away by a thought, you notice: 'There is a thought about tomorrow's meeting.' In that noticing, a little space appears between you and the thought. The book suggests that this space brings a sense of calm and freedom, because you are no longer entirely controlled by what the mind says.
Thoughts are not facts

When you observe thoughts, you may notice that many are not accurate. They are guesses, fears, habits or old stories. 'Everyone will think I'm stupid' is a thought, not a fact. Seeing thoughts as mental events rather than truths can loosen their emotional grip. You can still take useful thoughts seriously while letting go of unhelpful ones.
Simple ways to practise

You can practise watching the mind for short periods: sitting quietly for a minute and noticing whatever thoughts arise, without following them. Some people find it helpful to label thoughts gently, such as 'planning', 'worrying' or 'remembering'. Others focus on the breath and notice when thoughts pull them away. The aim is not to stop thinking, but to see thinking more clearly. Even a few moments of watching the mind during an ordinary day, such as while waiting for a kettle to boil, can be practice.
Using the thinking mind well

The book is not against thinking. Thinking is a powerful tool for solving problems, learning and creating. The suggestion is to use the mind as a tool when needed, rather than being used by it all the time. If thoughts feel overwhelming or distressing, please consider speaking with a qualified professional.

example.title: Illustrative example: the exam-night spiral
example.text: The night before a big exam, Ishaan, a student in Delhi, lay awake thinking, 'I'll fail, I'll disappoint everyone, my future is ruined.' He remembered the idea of watching thoughts. He said to himself, 'There's the worrying voice again.' He noticed that the thoughts were predictions, not facts. They did not vanish, but they felt a little less loud, and he was able to focus on his breathing until he fell asleep. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Many people experience a constant inner commentary.
You can observe thoughts rather than be carried away by them.
Thoughts are mental events, not necessarily facts.
Use thinking as a tool; seek support if thoughts feel overwhelming.
reflect: What does your inner voice say most often when you are stressed?
How might it feel to notice that voice rather than believe it immediately?

lessons.title: Accept what is, then act
cards: The book uses 'surrender' to mean accepting the present moment as it is.
It doesn't mean giving up; you can still take action to change things.
Accepting first can make your action calmer and clearer.
lessons.tryThis: Think of one small situation you are resisting, such as a delay or an inconvenience. Say to yourself, 'This is what is happening right now.' Take three slow breaths. Then ask, 'What, if anything, can I do next?' Take that one step, or let it be if there is nothing to do.

body.intro: When something unwanted happens, a natural reaction is resistance: 'This shouldn't be happening.' The Power of Now discusses acceptance, sometimes called surrender, as a way of meeting the present moment without inner fighting. This lesson explores what acceptance does and does not mean, and how it can coexist with taking action. This lesson summarises ideas from The Power of Now by Eckhart Tolle in our own words. It is reflective practice, not a treatment for anxiety or any condition.
sections: Resistance adds suffering

The book observes that much of our distress comes not only from difficult situations but from our resistance to them. Stuck in traffic, we fume. Facing bad news, we argue with reality in our heads. The book suggests that this mental resistance adds a layer of suffering on top of whatever is already hard, and it rarely changes the situation itself.
What acceptance means

Acceptance, as the book describes it, means fully acknowledging what is happening right now, without inner struggle against it. It is a shift from 'This shouldn't be' to 'This is what is happening.' Acceptance is about the present moment as it is, not about approving of it or giving up hope for change.
Acceptance and action

A common misunderstanding is that acceptance means passivity. The book clarifies that you can accept a situation and still act to change it. In fact, action taken from acceptance is often clearer and calmer than action taken from frustration or panic. If your roof is leaking, accepting that it is leaking lets you focus on fixing it rather than raging at the rain. Many people find that once they stop arguing with the situation in their head, they have more energy for whatever needs doing.
Situations you cannot change

Some things cannot be changed: a past event, another person's choice, a loss. Acceptance in these cases can bring a sense of peace that resistance cannot. It does not mean the feelings disappear. Grief and sadness are natural. Acceptance allows those feelings to be present without adding the extra burden of fighting them.
Gentleness and limits

Acceptance is not about tolerating harm or injustice. If you are in an unsafe situation, seeking help and making changes is important. Acceptance is a stance towards the present moment, not a reason to stay in harm's way. If acceptance feels impossible during a painful time, that is understandable; support from others or a qualified professional can help.

example.title: Illustrative example: the cancelled train
example.text: Geeta was travelling from Bhopal to Delhi for her niece's engagement when her train was cancelled. Her first reaction was anger and panic. After a few minutes of fuming, she took a breath and said to herself, 'The train is cancelled. That is what is happening.' With a calmer mind, she checked bus options, called her family to let them know, and found a seat on an evening bus. She arrived late, but less exhausted than if she had spent the journey angry. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Resistance to what is happening can add suffering on top of difficulty.
Acceptance means acknowledging the present without inner struggle.
Acceptance and action can go together; action from acceptance is often clearer.
Acceptance does not mean tolerating harm; seek help when needed.
reflect: What situation are you currently resisting in your mind?
What action might become clearer if you accepted that situation as it is right now?

lessons.title: Feel alive from the inside
cards: The book suggests bringing attention to the felt sense of aliveness in your body.
This can anchor you in the present when your mind is busy.
It is a reflective practice, not a medical treatment.
lessons.tryThis: Sit or lie comfortably for one minute. Bring attention to your hands and notice any sensation, such as warmth, tingling or heaviness. Then move attention to your feet. Keep your eyes open if that feels better. If this feels uncomfortable in any way, stop and focus on an outside anchor, like the feel of the chair.

body.intro: We usually experience our bodies from the outside: how they look, what they can do, where they hurt. The Power of Now describes another way: feeling the body from the inside, sensing the aliveness within. This lesson explores the book's idea of the 'inner body' as a gentle practice for grounding attention in the present. This lesson summarises ideas from The Power of Now by Eckhart Tolle in our own words. It is reflective practice, not a treatment for anxiety or any condition.
sections: What the inner body means

The book uses the phrase 'inner body' to describe the felt sense of being alive within your body, the subtle sensations of energy, warmth or tingling you can notice when you direct attention inward. Rather than thinking about your body, you feel it directly. The book presents this as a way to anchor attention in the present and step out of constant thinking.
Why it can help

When attention rests in the body, it is less available for anxious thinking. The book suggests that sensing the inner body can bring a sense of calm and groundedness. Many people notice something similar during activities like yoga, swimming or simply lying still: a sense of being 'here' rather than lost in thought.
A simple practice

One way to try this is to sit or lie comfortably, close your eyes, and bring attention to your hands. Notice any sensations without judging them. Then slowly move attention to your feet, arms, chest and face. You do not need to feel anything dramatic; simply noticing is enough. The practice can take a minute or longer. If at any point it feels uncomfortable, open your eyes and return to normal activity.
Inner body in daily life

The book suggests keeping some attention in the body even during ordinary activities: feeling your feet while standing in a queue, noticing your breath while waiting for a lift, sensing your hands while washing dishes. These moments can act as small anchors to the present throughout the day.
Body awareness with care

For some people, especially those with experiences of trauma or chronic pain, focusing on the body can be uncomfortable or distressing. That is understandable and nothing to push through. Keeping eyes open, focusing on external sensations like the feel of a chair, or skipping this practice entirely are all fine. A qualified professional can help if body awareness brings up difficult feelings.

example.title: Illustrative example: waiting at the clinic
example.text: Sudha sat in a crowded waiting room in Chennai for her mother's appointment, feeling anxious and restless. Instead of scrolling her phone, she placed her hands on her knees and gently noticed the warmth and weight of her hands, then her feet on the floor, then her breathing. Her worries did not disappear, but she felt steadier and more able to support her mother when they were called in. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: The 'inner body' refers to sensing aliveness within the body.
Resting attention in the body can anchor you in the present.
A simple scan from hands to feet takes only a minute.
If body focus feels distressing, use external anchors or skip it; seek support if needed.
reflect: Where in your body do you most easily notice sensation?
Which everyday waiting moment could become a short body-awareness pause?

lessons.title: Persuade without pressure
cards: The book's theme is getting good outcomes with people without bullying or being bullied.
It favours making others feel good about helping you.
Influence that respects the other person tends to last longer.
lessons.tryThis: Think of a current disagreement or request. Write down what you want, then what you think the other person wants and why. Ask them one open question to check. Then sketch one option that would give each of you something you value, and propose it politely.

body.intro: Persuasion often gets a bad name, associated with pushy salespeople or manipulative arguments. The Art of Persuasion, previously published as Winning Without Intimidation, takes a different view: the most effective persuasion helps everyone involved feel good about the outcome. This lesson explores persuasion as a respectful, win-win process. This lesson summarises ideas from The Art of Persuasion by Bob Burg in our own words.
sections: Persuasion without pressure

The book argues that intimidation, pressure and manipulation might get short-term results, but they damage relationships and trust. People who feel pushed often resist, or agree reluctantly and later back out. Persuasion that respects the other person, on the other hand, tends to produce agreements that last.
Win-win outcomes

A central idea is that the best outcomes are those where both sides feel they have gained something. Instead of thinking about how to 'win' over someone, you think about how to find a solution that meets both your needs. This might take more listening and creativity, but it creates goodwill and makes future cooperation easier.
Understanding the other person

To find a win-win solution, you need to understand what the other person wants and why. The book emphasises listening and asking questions before making your case. When people feel understood, they are more open to hearing your perspective. Assuming you already know what they want often leads to misunderstandings.

A useful habit is to ask open questions, ones that cannot be answered with a simple yes or no, such as 'What matters most to you here?' or 'What would a good outcome look like for you?' Then listen without interrupting. You may discover that the other person's real concern is different from what you assumed, and that a solution meeting both your needs is easier to find than it first seemed.
Making it easy to say yes

The book discusses how people are more likely to agree when they feel respected and when agreeing does not cause them to lose face. Offering choices, acknowledging their concerns, and framing requests politely can make it easier for someone to say yes without feeling cornered.
Ethics in persuasion

Respectful persuasion is honest. It does not hide information, exaggerate benefits or exploit someone's fears. If a solution truly is not good for the other person, it is better to acknowledge that than to push it through. Long-term trust is worth more than any single agreement. Persuasion that respects the other person's freedom to say no is, in the end, more persuasive than persuasion that tries to remove that freedom.

example.title: Illustrative example: the shop and the delivery delay
example.text: Rakesh ran a small electronics shop in Jaipur. A customer came in angry because a repaired phone was not ready on time. Rather than arguing, Rakesh listened, apologised for the delay, and asked what would help most. The customer needed the phone for a trip the next day. Rakesh offered a loaner phone for the trip and promised to call as soon as the repair was finished. The customer left satisfied, and later recommended the shop to friends. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Pressure may work short-term but damages trust.
Aim for outcomes where both sides gain something.
Listen and understand the other person before making your case.
Respectful persuasion is honest and makes it easy to say yes.
reflect: When did someone persuade you in a way that left you feeling respected?
In a current disagreement, what might a win-win outcome look like?

lessons.title: Steady yourself first
cards: The book stresses staying in control of your own reactions in tense moments.
Reacting from anger usually makes persuasion harder.
Calm gives you more choices in how to respond.
lessons.tryThis: Choose a short phrase to remind yourself of your goal in hard conversations, such as 'solve, not win'. The next time you feel a strong reaction, take one slow breath, say the phrase silently, and only then reply. Afterwards, do something to release the tension, such as a walk or a chat with a friend.

body.intro: It is hard to influence others when you are not in control of your own reactions. The Art of Persuasion emphasises that steadying yourself comes first. When you respond calmly rather than react emotionally, you are more likely to reach a good outcome. This lesson explores how managing your own emotions supports better conversations. This lesson summarises ideas from The Art of Persuasion by Bob Burg in our own words.
sections: Reacting versus responding

The book distinguishes between reacting, an immediate, often emotional reply, and responding, a considered choice of words and actions. When someone is rude or unfair, the urge to react is strong. But reacting often escalates conflict and makes it harder to reach any agreement. Responding means pausing long enough to choose a path that serves your goals.
You control your side

You cannot control how others behave, but you can control how you respond. The book suggests that this is actually a source of strength. Instead of letting another person's mood dictate yours, you can stay steady. This calm often influences the other person too; it is hard to keep shouting at someone who is speaking quietly and respectfully.
Simple ways to steady yourself

Practical techniques include taking a slow breath before replying, silently counting to a few, relaxing your shoulders, or briefly stepping away if needed. Reminding yourself of your goal, for example 'I want to solve this problem, not win an argument', can also help. These small actions create space for a better response. With practice, these small pauses become more natural, and you may find that conversations which once felt tense become easier to handle with a clear head.
Not taking it personally

The book notes that when people behave badly, it often reflects their own stress, fear or frustration rather than anything about you. This does not excuse poor behaviour, but recognising it can make it easier not to take it personally, and therefore easier to stay calm. Seeing difficult behaviour this way can turn a moment of anger into a moment of understanding, which makes a calm reply much easier to find.
Caring for yourself afterwards

Staying calm in a difficult conversation can be draining. Afterwards, it helps to release the tension: talk to a friend, take a walk, or simply rest. Managing emotions is not about suppressing them permanently, but about choosing when and how to express them.

example.title: Illustrative example: the angry parent at school
example.text: Anjali, a primary school teacher in Nagpur, was confronted by a parent who accused her of being unfair to his son. She felt her heart pound and wanted to defend herself sharply. Instead, she took a breath and said, 'I can see you're upset. Let's sit down and talk about what happened.' As she listened, the parent calmed down, and together they agreed on a plan to support the child. That evening, she took a long walk to unwind. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Responding thoughtfully works better than reacting emotionally.
You cannot control others, but you can control your response.
A pause, a breath or a reminder of your goal can steady you.
Others' bad behaviour often reflects their stress; take care of yourself afterwards.
reflect: In what kind of situation do you tend to react rather than respond?
What small action could help you pause next time?

lessons.title: Kindness with difficult people
cards: The book suggests that firm kindness often works better than confrontation.
Letting someone save face can calm a tense exchange.
Being kind doesn't mean giving up your position.
lessons.tryThis: Before your next interaction with a difficult person, prepare one sentence that acknowledges their feelings and one that offers them a graceful way out, such as 'I can see why it looked that way.' Use them calmly. If the behaviour becomes abusive, set a clear limit and seek help.

body.intro: Everyone encounters difficult people: a demanding boss, a rude customer, a critical relative. The Art of Persuasion suggests that kindness, tact and patience, rather than force, are often the most effective ways to handle them. This lesson explores how to deal with difficult people while protecting your dignity and theirs. This lesson summarises ideas from The Art of Persuasion by Bob Burg in our own words.
sections: Why kindness works

When faced with rudeness, it is tempting to respond in kind. The book argues that kindness, delivered calmly, often disarms difficult people more effectively. People expect resistance; when they meet courtesy instead, they may soften. Kindness here does not mean weakness or giving in; it means staying respectful while holding your position.
Letting people save face

The book emphasises allowing others to save face, giving them a way to back down without feeling humiliated. If you corner someone or prove them wrong publicly, they are likely to dig in. Offering a graceful way out, such as 'I can see why it seemed that way', makes it easier for them to change course.

Saving face matters in many settings, including workplaces and families where respect and seniority carry weight. Correcting an elder or a senior colleague privately rather than in front of others, or framing a disagreement as a shared problem ('Maybe we both missed something here'), can make it far easier for them to accept a different view. The goal is not to win the point, but to reach a better outcome while keeping the relationship intact.
Acknowledging feelings

Difficult behaviour often comes from frustration or feeling unheard. Acknowledging feelings, for example 'I understand this has been frustrating for you', can lower tension even before you address the actual problem. People who feel heard are more open to solutions.
Setting limits

Kindness does not mean tolerating abuse. If someone is threatening, harassing or repeatedly disrespectful, it is appropriate to set clear limits, end the conversation, or seek help from a manager, authority or trusted person. Your safety and dignity matter. It is also fine to recognise that some people will remain difficult no matter how kindly you behave. Your aim is to act in line with your own values, not to force a change in theirs.
Thinking long-term

With people you will see again, such as colleagues, neighbours or relatives, the way you handle one difficult moment can shape the relationship for years. Responding with patience and respect, even when it is hard, often builds a foundation of trust that makes future interactions easier.

example.title: Illustrative example: the irate neighbour
example.text: Mr. Kapoor, Deepa's neighbour in a Delhi housing society, complained loudly that her car was blocking his gate. In fact, it was a visitor's car. Deepa felt defensive but chose kindness: 'I'm sorry for the trouble, I can see how frustrating that is. It's not my car, but let me help find the owner.' Mr. Kapoor, surprised, calmed down and even apologised for shouting. Their relationship became friendlier afterwards. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: Calm kindness often disarms difficult behaviour.
Let others save face so they can change course without humiliation.
Acknowledge feelings before addressing the problem.
Kindness includes setting limits when behaviour becomes abusive.
reflect: Who is a difficult person in your life, and what might be driving their behaviour?
How could you offer them a way to save face in your next interaction?

lessons.title: Influence grows from trust
cards: The book links influence to relationships built over time.
People are more open to those they know, like and trust.
Small, genuine acts of attention build that trust.
lessons.tryThis: This week, offer three small courtesies without expecting anything back: remember and use someone's name, follow up on something they mentioned, or share something useful. Also keep one small promise exactly as you said you would. Notice how these moments feel and how people respond.

body.intro: Influence is not something you switch on during a negotiation. The Art of Persuasion suggests that people are most open to those they know, like and trust, and that this trust is built gradually through everyday interactions. This lesson explores how rapport and genuine relationships create the foundation for positive influence. This lesson summarises ideas from The Art of Persuasion by Bob Burg in our own words.
sections: Know, like and trust

The book returns often to the idea that people prefer to cooperate with, help and do business with those they know, like and trust. These qualities are not created by clever words in a single conversation. They grow through consistent behaviour over time: being reliable, honest, respectful and genuinely interested in others.
Building rapport

Rapport is a sense of connection and mutual understanding. It can be built by showing genuine interest in people, remembering details they share, listening attentively, and finding common ground. Small courtesies, like using someone's name, thanking them sincerely, or following up on something they mentioned, add up over time.

Rapport is not about pretending to agree or copying someone's opinions. It grows from honest curiosity. Asking about someone's weekend, their family or their hometown, and actually remembering the answer, signals that you see them as a person and not just a role. In a busy workplace, these small human moments are often what people remember most.
Giving before asking

The book emphasises focusing on providing value to others rather than on what you can get. Helping a colleague, sharing useful information, or introducing people who might benefit from knowing each other builds goodwill. When the time comes to ask for something, people are more willing to help someone who has been generous with them. This should come from genuine care, not calculation. Generosity that expects nothing back is usually the kind people remember and return.
Consistency matters

Trust can take a long time to build and a short time to damage. Keeping promises, being on time, admitting mistakes and treating people fairly, even when no one is watching, all contribute to a reputation for trustworthiness. Inconsistency, such as being friendly only when you need something, quickly erodes it. When you do slip, as everyone does, owning it quickly and sincerely tends to repair trust faster than excuses.
Relationships beyond work

These principles apply in families, friendships and communities too. Being someone who listens, keeps their word and treats others with respect makes relationships richer, quite apart from any question of influence.

example.title: Illustrative example: the helpful colleague
example.text: In a busy call centre in Kolkata, Sourav was known for helping new joiners learn the systems, even though it was not part of his job. He remembered their names, checked in on how they were settling, and shared tips. When he later proposed a new process to reduce call waiting times, his colleagues were quick to support it, partly because the idea was good and partly because they trusted him. This is an illustrative story.

takeaways: People cooperate more with those they know, like and trust.
Rapport grows from genuine interest, listening and small courtesies.
Give value before asking, from genuine care rather than calculation.
Consistency builds trust; inconsistency erodes it quickly.
reflect: Who do you trust most, and what did they do to earn that trust?
What small courtesy could you offer someone at work or home this week?
